paragraphs.text: [Muzha](muzha:where-it-is) is a hill district on the southeast edge of Taipei, in Wenshan District, where the tea grows on low slopes of a few hundred metres. Fujian settlers brought Tieguanyin here from [Anxi](muzha:history) in the late nineteenth century. The trade most often credits the tea master Zhang Naimiao, who planted it in the Zhanghu part of Muzha in 1895. The [traditional Muzha style](taiwan-oolong:muzha) is a more oxidised oolong, roasted over charcoal, its leaf wrapped in cloth and rolled again and again. On a label, Muzha names [a place and a way of making](muzha:on-a-label). It does not prove which plant the leaf came from.

This tea dates from 1972, which makes it fifty-four years old. Taiwan has a tradition of keeping oolong for years, called [lao cha, old tea](taiwan-oolong:ageing). Leaf chosen for keeping starts well roasted and dry. It is roasted again at low heat from time to time, because over the years it takes in moisture that has to be driven out. No standard says when an oolong becomes old. Those who give a figure put it between ten and thirty years, and this tea is well past the longer of the two.

brewing.text: Ball-rolled Taiwan oolong takes hot water, about 90 to 100°C, a fairly generous amount of leaf and short steeps; the balls open slowly and give many infusions. Roasted Dong Ding takes water from about 95°C to a full boil. Aged oolong takes very hot water, in a pot that holds its heat, clay above all. Oriental Beauty is the exception and takes cooler water, about 80 to 95°C.

notice.text: A smooth, mellow, thick cup with little astringency, often plum or prune, sometimes something like medicinal herbs or ginseng, and an amber to red-brown liquor.
